questions.question: Who speaks on Wednesday?
questions.solution: B is on Thursday, so the C–E pair is Mon–Tue, Tue–Wed or Fri–Sat, and D can't be on Wed or Fri. If A is on Saturday: C–E on Mon–Tue leaves Wed and Fri for D and F (D can't take either). C–E on Tue–Wed gives D Mon, F Fri, but then A (Sat) and F (Fri) are consecutive Physics talks. So A is on Monday. C–E on Tue–Wed leaves Fri and Sat, with D forced to Sat and F after D, which is impossible. So C–E = Fri–Sat, D = Tue, F = Wed. Subjects: A, F Physics (Mon, Wed are not consecutive ✓). E (Sat) is Economics and the other Economics must be adjacent, so C (Fri). D (Tue) is History, as is B. Final: Mon A (Physics), Tue D (History), Wed F (Physics), Thu B (History), Fri C (Economics), Sat E (Economics).

questions.question: With 20 coins, how many coins must Asha remove on her first turn to be sure of winning?
questions.solution: Work backwards: a pile is 'losing' for the player to move if every move leads to a winning pile. 0 is losing. 1, 2 and 4 can reach 0, so they're winning. 3 → 2 or 1 only, so it's losing. In general, the losing piles are exactly the multiples of 3, because 1, 2 and 4 are never multiples of 3. 20 − 2 = 18 is a multiple of 3. Taking 1 (19) or 4 (16) leaves a winning pile for Bilal.

questions.question: For how many starting pile sizes from 1 to 30 (inclusive) can Bilal force a win?
questions.solution: Work backwards: a pile is 'losing' for the player to move if every move leads to a winning pile. 0 is losing. 1, 2 and 4 can reach 0, so they're winning. 3 → 2 or 1 only, so it's losing. In general, the losing piles are exactly the multiples of 3, because 1, 2 and 4 are never multiples of 3. Bilal wins exactly when the start is a multiple of 3: 3, 6, …, 30, which is 10 sizes.

questions.question: Under the standard rule, what is the smallest starting pile larger than 20 with which Bilal can force a win?
questions.solution: Work backwards: a pile is 'losing' for the player to move if every move leads to a winning pile. 0 is losing. 1, 2 and 4 can reach 0, so they're winning. 3 → 2 or 1 only, so it's losing. In general, the losing piles are exactly the multiples of 3, because 1, 2 and 4 are never multiples of 3. The next multiple of 3 after 20 is 21.

questions.question: Suppose players may remove 1, 2, 3 or 4 coins (last coin still wins). With 23 coins, how many should Asha remove first to be sure of winning?
questions.solution: With moves 1–4, the losing piles are multiples of 5 (any move from 5k can be answered to return to 5(k − 1)). Asha should leave 20, so she takes 3.

questions.question: Now suppose the rule is reversed: the player who takes the last coin LOSES (moves are still 1, 2 or 4). With 10 coins, how many should Asha remove first to be sure of winning?
questions.solution: Now a pile of 1 is losing for the player to move, because they must take the last coin. Working upward: 2, 3 → can leave 1, so winning. 4 → leaves 3, 2 or 0, and 0 means you just took the last coin and lost, so 4 is losing. The losing piles are 1, 4, 7, 10, 13, … (one more than a multiple of 3). 10 is losing: from 10, Asha can leave 9, 8 or 6, and each lets Bilal move back to 7. So she cannot force a win.

questions.question: How many chocolates did Q get?
questions.solution: Let T = t, so S = t + 1. Let R = r, so Q = 2r and P = 2r + t. Total: (2r + t) + 2r + r + (t + 1) + t = 5r + 3t + 1 = 24 ⇒ 5r + 3t = 23. Options: (r, t) = (4, 1) or (1, 6). R > S rules out (1, 6) (R = 1 < S = 7). So P = 9, Q = 8, R = 4, S = 2, T = 1.

questions.question: What is the code? (Enter all four digits.)
questions.solution: (1) 2054 says exactly one of 2, 0, 5, 4 is in the code. 3520 says two of 3, 5, 2, 0 are, so 3 is in the code plus exactly one of 5, 2, 0, and 4 is out. (2) 9361 needs two of 9, 3, 6, 1, so one of 9, 6, 1 (call it y). 8697 needs two of 8, 6, 9, 7. If y = 1, there's no room for two of those, so y is 9 or 6 and the 4th digit (z) is 8 or 7. (3) 7148: exactly one digit, in place, so z sits where 7148 has it (7 → 1st place, 8 → 4th place). 1 is out. (4) 1052: one digit in place, so the digit x from {5, 2, 0} is where 1052 has it: 0 → 2nd, 5 → 3rd, 2 → 4th. But 2054 says x is misplaced there: 0 would be 2nd and 5 would be 3rd in both guesses, a contradiction. So x = 2 in 4th place, which forces z = 7 in 1st place. (5) The code is 7 _ _ 2 with 3 and y in the middle. 9361 needs exactly one in place: 7362 gives two in place and 7632 gives none, so y = 9. 7932 gives none in place, but 7392 gives 3 in place and 9 misplaced ✓. 8697 then gives 9 in place and 7 misplaced ✓. Code = 7392 (a computer check of all 4,536 possible codes confirms it's the only one).

questions.question: Who won Round 3?
questions.solution: R1 winner is X and Z is last. Each round has a different winner, so Y wins exactly one of R2/R3. Y = 10 = 4 + 3 + 3, so Y is 2nd in the other two rounds, giving R1: X, Y, W, Z. X = 4 + (R2 points) + 1 must be 8, 7 or 5, so X is 2nd (X = 8) or 3rd (X = 7) in R2. Case Y wins R3: R2's winner is Z (Z must be ahead of W) and Y is 2nd, so X is 3rd (X = 7) and W 4th. Then W and Z must total 8 and 5. Z = 1 + 4 + (2 or 3) ≥ 7, so Z = 8 and W = 5, contradicting W > Z. So Y wins R2. If R2 = Y, Z, X, W, then X = 7, and R3 (won by W or Z) makes either W = 7 (a repeat of X's 7) or W < Z. So R2 = Y, X, Z, W and X = 8. R3 = winner, Y, other, X. cd-houses.title: Four houses
cd-houses.html:
Four houses

Kiran, Leela, Manav and Nisha live in four houses numbered 1 to 4 in a row. Each owns a different pet (cat, dog, parrot, fish) and drives a different coloured car (red, blue, white, black).

  • Kiran and Nisha live in the two end houses.
  • Leela owns the parrot. Kiran owns the fish.
  • The fish lives in house 1, and the white car belongs to house 4.
  • Manav drives the black car and does not own the cat.
  • The red car belongs to the house immediately to the right of (one number higher than) the dog's house.

cd-seminar.html:
Seminar week

Six professors, A to F, each give one talk at a seminar running Monday to Saturday, one talk per day. Two talks are on Economics, two on History and two on Physics.

  • B speaks on Thursday, on History.
  • C speaks on the day immediately before E.
  • A speaks on either Monday or Saturday, on Physics.
  • F speaks on some day after D, and D does not speak on a day adjacent to B's.
  • The two Economics talks are on consecutive days, but no two Physics talks are.
  • C's talk is not on History. E speaks on Economics and F on Physics.

cd-choc.title: Sharing chocolates
cd-choc.html:
Sharing chocolates

24 chocolates were shared among five friends P, Q, R, S and T. Each got at least one, and no two got the same number.

  • Q got twice as many as R.
  • S got exactly one more than T.
  • P got as many as Q and T together, and P got the most.
  • R got more than S.

cd-coins.title: Coin game
cd-coins.html:
Coin game

Asha and Bilal play a game with a pile of coins. They take turns, Asha first. On each turn a player must remove 1, 2 or 4 coins (never more than the pile holds). Under the standard rule, the player who takes the last coin wins. Both players always play perfectly.

cd-league.title: Five-team league
cd-league.html:
Five-team league

Five teams A, B, C, D and E played a league in which every team played every other team exactly once. A win earned 3 points, a draw 1 point and a loss 0.
